items.summary: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube , ai , generative-ai , llms , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai-misuse

items.summary: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code , which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT() . Via Lobste.rs Tags: mysql , postgresql , replication , scaling , wikipedia , ai-security-research

items.summary: Release: llm-gemini 0.38 Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon . I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse. Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price , and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires. The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up: So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen. Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st. I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high. I dropped Argon from my Gemini 4 comparison grid - here's the new Gemini 4 lineup, where the Neon pelicans do look better than Hydrogen and worse than Carbon: As I've done with several recent models , I also fired the following prompt against Gemini 4 Neon on "extra" effort level in Google Antigravity: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's the result . items.summary: Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0 Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats. I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it. Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot. Add the plugin to Datasette ( datasette install datasette-arrows ) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option: This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release. Tags: datasette , projects

items.summary: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. Tags: sandboxing , security , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , claude-code , codex , pi

items.summary: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra . The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here , but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra . Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon . This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time: I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different models I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned. Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels Then later: OK make it 20s Here's the exported transcript . The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example: When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on . I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?"
